questions.q: How does General Ledger undo the effect of a posted journal?
options: By directly editing the posted journal's lines
By deleting the posted journal
By creating a brand-new reversal journal with the opposite effect
By changing the ledger's currency
questions.explain: Since posted journals are read-only, a reversal is a new journal entry that cancels out the original.

questions.q: What does the 'switch debit/credit' reversal method do?
options: Deletes the original journal
Negates the amount while keeping the same designation
Changes the journal's category to Reversal
Swaps each line's debit/credit designation on the same accounts
questions.explain: Switch debit/credit flips each line's designation — debits become credits and vice versa.

questions.q: What does the 'change sign' reversal method do differently from switch debit/credit?
options: It keeps each line's debit/credit designation but enters the amount as negative
It changes the account combination entirely
It posts to a different ledger
It requires a different approval workflow
questions.explain: Change sign keeps the original designation and negates the amount, reaching the same net effect through a different mechanism.

questions.q: Why is an accrual journal typically flagged to auto-reverse next period?
options: Because accruals can never be posted otherwise
So the accrual's effect is automatically backed out once the real invoice posts, without anyone needing to remember to reverse it manually
Because auto-reverse is required for all journals regardless of purpose
Because it changes the journal's source to Payables
questions.explain: Auto-reverse ensures the accrual is cleanly backed out when the real transaction posts, avoiding double-counting and manual follow-up.

questions.q: Which period choices are available when reversing a journal?
options: Only the same period
Only the next period
Reversals cannot be assigned to a period
Same period, next period, or a specific period
questions.explain: A reversal can be posted to the same period, the next period, or a specific chosen period.
